title: Training Together Builds Team Memory
text:
Should team members be trained individually or together? Diane Wei Liang, Richard Moreland and Linda Argote, at Carnegie Mellon University and the University of Pittsburgh, tested this with a hands-on task: assembling a transistor radio from a kit.

Participants were trained to build the radio either alone or in the groups of three that they would later work in. A week later, each group was asked to assemble the radio together, without instructions. The researchers measured how well the groups recalled the steps and how many errors their finished radios had.

Groups whose members had been trained together recalled more about how to build the radio and made fewer errors. Observing videotapes of the sessions, the researchers found that these groups showed more signs of what is called transactive memory: members knew who was good at what, trusted each other's knowledge, and coordinated smoothly. Each member specialized in part of the task, and the others relied on that.
lesson: Teams work better when members know who knows what. Train people together on the actual work, so they learn each other's strengths along with the task.
people: Diane Wei Liang, Richard Moreland, Linda Argote
location: Carnegie Mellon University and University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, USA
source: Liang, D. W., Moreland, R., and Argote, L. (1995). Group versus individual training and group performance: The mediating role of transactive memory. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 21(4), 384-393.
